subtopic: Reaching a fitness or sports goal
subtype: Approach: doing too much too soon [Pitfall]
passage: “Disha, you asked how I ended up on the bench, so here it is. I'm Aman, and I wanted the school football team more than anything. I thought more was better. From day one I trained twice a day, once before school, once after. My legs felt sore by the third day. I told myself sore meant working. When my thigh started pulling, I taped it and carried on. In week two something gave way on the field, a proper strain. The coach said I needed rest and should see a doctor if it kept going. I missed the whole trial period. I wanted to speed everything up, and it cost me weeks instead of saving me any.”

qa.q: How many times a day did Aman train?
How does Aman feel now about the choice?
qa.a: Frustrated and regretful: wanting to hurry things up cost weeks instead of saving them.

qa.q: What could Aman do differently next time, and why?
qa.a: Build up slowly with rest days and listen to soreness, since steady training keeps Aman on the field.

qa.q: How does the injury look to Aman's coach?
qa.a: Aman's coach sees an eager player who ignored warning signs, and probably wishes Aman had spoken up when the soreness began.

grounding: A teen aiming for the school team trains twice daily from day one, ignores soreness and picks up a strain.

subtopic: Reaching a fitness or sports goal
subtype: Approach: doing too much too soon [Pitfall]
passage:
I'm Jaya, and Harish lives two doors down, so I see him leave in the mornings. The school football trials were a month away. On the first day of the holidays he was out at five-thirty, running, and again at six in the evening, sprints and jumping on the stairs. Twice a day, from day one.
By the end of the first week he was walking strangely down the stairs. I asked if he was okay. “Just sore. Pain means it's working,” he said, and went out again.
On day ten I heard him shout from the ground. His father helped him home, one arm over his shoulder. The doctor said it was a thigh strain, and no running for several weeks.
The trials came and went. Harish watched from the side, sitting on the steps with his leg out. I don't know what he was thinking. He didn't say much that day.

qa.q: What did Harish say when asked if he was okay?
qa.a: Just sore. Pain means it's working.

qa.q: How might Harish have felt watching the trials from the side?
qa.a: He was probably frustrated and disappointed, missing the very goal he trained so hard to reach sooner.

qa.q: What could Harish have done instead from day one?
qa.a: Start with one gentler session a day and rest days, building up slowly and treating lasting soreness as a sign to ease off and ask a coach.

qa.q: How did the month look to Jaya?
qa.a: Jaya saw early enthusiasm turn into limping and then sitting on the steps, without knowing what Harish felt inside.

grounding: A neighbour sees a teen train twice daily from day one for trials, ignore soreness, and pick up a strain that keeps him out for weeks.

subtopic: Reaching a fitness or sports goal
subtype: Approach: doing too much too soon [Pitfall]
passage:
Day 1: Francis wants a place on the school basketball team, with selection in three weeks. He writes a plan: shooting at six in the morning, sprints and jumps at six in the evening, every day. His elder brother Thomas says, “Every day? From today?” Francis nods.
Day 6: His calves burn on the stairs. His knees ache when he sits. He tells himself soreness is just weakness leaving, and adds fifty more jumps.
Day 9: In the evening session, on the fortieth jump, something pulls at the back of his ankle. He can't put weight on it. Thomas carries his bag home. The clinic doctor says it's a strain: rest, no jumping for several weeks, and come back if it isn't getting better.
Selection day: Francis sits in the stands with his ankle strapped, watching others try out for the spot he tried to rush toward.

qa.q: What did the clinic doctor say?
qa.a: It's a strain: rest, no jumping for several weeks, and come back if it isn't getting better.

qa.q: What was Francis telling himself on day 6, and what does it suggest?
qa.a: That soreness is just weakness leaving; it suggests he felt determined and impatient, too eager to listen to the pain.

qa.q: Which approach would have suited Francis better with three weeks to go?
qa.a: One session a day with rest days and skill practice, easing off when soreness lingered, so he reached selection fit rather than injured.

qa.q: How might Thomas see those three weeks?
qa.a: Thomas, who questioned "every day from today", probably feels worried and sad watching his brother's rush end in the stands.

grounding: Shows a teen training twice daily from day one for team selection, ignoring soreness, and getting a strain that keeps him out.
